title: Alpha-1 receptors: agonists and alpha-blockers
ariaLabel: Schematic of a sympathetic nerve terminal releasing noradrenaline onto two cells that both carry alpha-1 receptors coupled to Gq: a blood vessel smooth muscle cell and a smooth muscle cell of the prostate and bladder neck. Each receptor activates phospholipase C and raises calcium, which contracts the muscle. An alpha-1 agonist adds to the signal, a non-selective alpha-1 blocker relaxes both cells, and an alpha-1A selective blocker mainly relaxes the prostate.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. A sympathetic nerve terminal and two target cells drawn side by side to compare tissues. Response levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or affinity is shown or implied.

blockInfo: An alpha-1 blocker molecule (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape) in the receptor's binding pocket. It occupies the pocket without activating the receptor, so noradrenaline cannot bind where it sits. The block is competitive: a lot of noradrenaline can partly outcompete it. The brightness of the symbol shows how many receptors it holds.
agonistInfo: An alpha-1 agonist molecule (generic teaching symbol) in the binding pocket. It activates the receptor like noradrenaline does, adding to the natural signal.

terminal.label: sympathetic nerve terminal
terminal.info: Sympathetic nerve terminal (a varicosity). Noradrenaline is packed into vesicles and released by exocytosis; most is taken back up by the noradrenaline transporter (not drawn).

molecule.name: noradrenaline

molecule.info: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine), 4-(2-amino-1-hydroxyethyl)benzene-1,2-diol, C8H11NO3 (PubChem CID 439260): a catechol ring with an ethanolamine side chain. Flat skeletal formula, bond angles and lengths drawn schematically; stereochemistry is not shown. In the cleft below it is drawn as a small bright dot.

info.cell: Vascular smooth muscle cell of an arteriole or vein, patch of its membrane in flat cross-section, schematic and not to scale. Alpha-1 receptors are the main route by which sympathetic nerves and circulating catecholamines constrict vessels.
info.rec: Alpha-1 adrenoceptor (α1): a seven-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptor coupled to Gαq. Noradrenaline binds from outside. The α1A, α1B and α1D subtypes are not distinguished in vessels here.
info.end: Calcium: IP3 from phospholipase C opens calcium release channels on the endoplasmic reticulum, and the rise in calcium contracts the smooth muscle through calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase (drawn: the node lights up). Diacylglycerol and protein kinase C are not drawn.

info.cell: Smooth muscle cell of the prostate or bladder neck, patch of its membrane. The α1A subtype is the main one here; its contraction narrows the urethra. Drawn beside the vessel cell only to compare tissues.
info.rec: Alpha-1A adrenoceptor: the α1 subtype that predominates in prostatic and bladder neck smooth muscle, coupled to Gαq. Blockers that prefer α1A relax these tissues with less effect on vessels.
info.end: Calcium: IP3 from phospholipase C releases calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum, and the smooth muscle contracts (drawn: the node lights up).

sources: Alpha-1 receptors and the Gq pathway. Alpha-1 receptors signal through Gq: phospholipase C splits PIP2 into IP3 and DAG, and IP3 releases calcium from stores, which contracts smooth muscle. Phenylephrine is a direct-acting alpha-1 agonist that constricts veins and arteries and raises blood pressure with little effect on cardiac muscle (Alpha-1 receptor agonists, NCBI Bookshelf).

Alpha-1 blockers. Alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, silodosin, tamsulosin and terazosin are selective alpha-1 blockers used for benign prostatic hyperplasia and hypertension; doxazosin, prazosin and terazosin cause more orthostatic hypotension, while alfuzosin, tamsulosin and silodosin affect the vasculature less and are first-line for prostatic symptoms (Selective alpha-blockers, StatPearls).
simplified: Only the alpha-1 receptor is drawn: alpha-2 receptors (presynaptic autoreceptors, clonidine), beta receptors, the individual alpha-1 subtypes in each tissue, non-competitive blockers (phenoxybenzamine), reflex responses to a change in blood pressure, ejaculation effects and first-dose hypotension are left out. The two cells are drawn side by side only to compare tissues. Levels, the size of the block and timing are illustrative; protein shapes are cartoons, not structures. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
